EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Persistent instability in the Western Hemisphere has often pulled Washington’s attention away from its priority foreign policy aims around the world. Within the region, the United States should focus its attention and resources on the foreign problems most likely to become domestic vulnerabilities. The United States has long prioritized migration, organized crime, infrastructure failures, and political instability in Canada or Mexico, recognizing they can quickly become domestic concerns, and has conceptually grouped the rest of the Western Hemisphere together as a lesser-prioritized single strategic unit.

That framing misreads the interconnected nature of migration routes, transnational criminal networks, supply chains, transportation networks, and sources of power for new technologies, and the consequences of China’s growing influence in America’s neighborhood. The United States is much more directly and quickly affected by dynamics in countries north of the Amazon River than in the region south of it. U.S. strategy should, therefore, revise its conception of prioritized geography to focus on Greater North America, spanning Canada, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and the Caribbean-facing countries of South America.

Over the next decade, U.S. policy should aim to make Greater North America a stronger economic base for American power. Washington should harness its proximity, trade, diaspora ties, and decades of security cooperation to help the countries in Greater North America become stronger economic and security partners. Instead of treating trade, migration, counternarcotics, development, and competition with outside powers as separate portfolios, U.S. policymakers should approach them as integrated challenges.

To do so, U.S. policymakers should focus on increased integration and resilience within Greater North America by prioritizing:

- Expanding trade to facilitate greater economic integration;
- Increasing investment to reduce supply-chain risk and counter Chinese influence;
- Reforming labor law to help fill legal U.S. work opportunities;
- Securing vulnerable infrastructure against hostile actors and natural disasters; and
- Restructuring the U.S. bureaucracy for a Greater North American orientation.

Given that many of the countries prioritized under a Greater North American strategy hold historical distrust of Washington, U.S. policymakers should give them good reasons to choose the United States: financing, dependable market access, and commitments that will survive a change of administration. A more resilient neighborhood would leave Washington with greater capacity to invest, compete, and lead globally.

INTRODUCTION

U.S. policy is being pulled in two opposing directions. On the one hand, the United States seeks to advance U.S. leadership and foreign policy priorities around the world, while on the other, persistent instability in the Western Hemisphere pulls Washington’s attention and resources back toward its own borders. Simply put, what happens in the countries closest to the United States can quickly become a domestic concern. Migration, narcotics flows, transnational crime, and illicit financing are all examples of this phenomenon. Washington confronts each crisis as it arises and as a separate issue, but that is not a sustainable approach. U.S. strategy should, therefore, prioritize creating stronger economic and security partners across a Greater North America, spanning Canada, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and the Caribbean-facing countries of South America.

This new strategy would include countries that are deeply integrated with the United States—principally Canada and Mexico—as well as those countries whose instability, infrastructure, or security directly affects the United States. Determining which countries have direct consequences for the United States requires examining complex, interconnected chains. For example, migration originating in Venezuela can move through Colombia, Panama, Central America, and Mexico before arriving at the U.S. border. Drugs produced in South America transit through the Caribbean and Central America and flow to Mexican organizations before they reach American consumers, a trade fueled by U.S. firearms and illicit finance along the way. Instability in Haiti quickly becomes a problem for the Coast Guard and the Department of Homeland Security. Who controls the ports, power systems, telecommunications networks, and cable landing stations in the Caribbean matters for U.S. economic security. Countries farther south, beyond the Amazon, are also important. Brazil plays a global role, Chile and Peru are integrated into U.S. critical-mineral supply chains, and Argentina exports beef and oil to the United States. Yet events in those countries rarely reach the United States as quickly or as directly as developments north of the Amazon. Farther south, Washington generally has time to decide how to engage. Inside Greater North America, events often make that choice for it.

THE STRATEGIC CONTEXT: CRISES NORTH OF THE AMAZON QUICKLY BECOME DOMESTIC PROBLEMS

The United States emerged from the Cold War with overwhelming economic and geopolitical advantages throughout the Western Hemisphere. Democratic government was spreading, American trade and investment dominated much of the region, and no other power could offer comparable bilateral economic benefits. Accordingly, the United States grew close to Canada and Mexico, signing the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) in 1992. But as transnational crime and insecurity in Central America and the Caribbean began to impact the United States, foreign policy thinkers began calling for a North American response to Central American insecurity and greater cooperation in the Caribbean. Those voices were largely ignored. Over the past two decades, developments in Venezuela and the Caribbean have made the limits of a three-country strategy—that is, one focused on the United States, Canada, and Mexico—harder to ignore.

Venezuela illustrates what happens when the United States ignores the domestic effects of events north of the Amazon. During the Biden administration, hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans already displaced to Colombia and Peru headed north after the pandemic eliminated job opportunities in the informal sector. This turned a crisis emanating from Caracas into a challenge at the U.S.-Mexico border. By the end of 2025, Venezuela’s political, economic, and security crisis had driven away nearly 7.9 million people, more than 6.9 million of whom had gone to Latin America and the Caribbean. The U.S. operation that removed President Nicolás Maduro from office in January 2026 did not dismantle the criminal networks built under Chavismo or resolve the conditions that drove migration. Going forward, only sustained reform of Venezuelan institutions can resolve those problems.

Over the past two decades, Beijing has become increasingly assertive around the world, including in the Western Hemisphere. Although the United States cannot compete with China everywhere, it should at least aim to be the partner of choice in Greater North America. Washington’s advantages in proximity, trade, diaspora ties, and decades of security cooperation have been challenged by Beijing’s steady diplomatic engagement, financing, and infrastructure projects. That dynamic has translated into Chinese influence over ports, telecommunications networks, and other critical systems that are close to the United States and interconnected with U.S. interests. Caribbean governments, for example, have responded to the offers before them, and Washington’s engagement has too often been patchy.

Over the next five to ten years, U.S. policymakers will struggle to separate strategic competition from regional instability; in this period, the world economy is likely to become less organized around efficiency and more around resilience and reliability. U.S. officials will be challenged to respond to the demands of artificial intelligence (AI) for reliable electricity, computing infrastructure, secure fiber, and data centers. AI, combined with new financial tools, will empower criminal groups and increase insecurity. At the same time, climate shocks will place greater pressure on Caribbean and Central American populations, and migration routes will shift in response to changing policies and conditions.

The United States will confront those pressures under greater fiscal constraints and with more domestic skepticism about foreign commitments than at any point since the Cold War. Washington, therefore, must prioritize its focus. Intense concentration on Canada and Mexico while neglecting the rest of the Western Hemisphere misunderstands geography and the nature of the U.S. relationship with the countries of the region. It also does little to help Washington decide where to focus its limited attention and resources.

U.S. INTERESTS AND OBJECTIVES

The United States should focus its attention and resources on those foreign problems that are most likely to become domestic problems. Canada and Mexico are the obvious starting points, due to their economic interdependence. In 2025, the United States traded approximately $1.84 trillion in goods and services with Canada and Mexico; as such, a major rupture in either relationship would have widespread effects on the U.S. economy. The fallout of the recent tariff fight with Canada has demonstrated the extent of this economic interdependence.

Problems in Mexico and Central America can increase migration, creating opportunities for criminal groups to exploit. For example, Haiti’s continued collapse could trigger maritime migration, requiring emergency U.S. action. Problems in Panama, which controls the canal linking the Atlantic and Pacific, can disrupt global trade, as the severe drought that forced restrictions on canal traffic in 2023 demonstrated. Meanwhile, Colombia cooperates with the United States on counternarcotics operations, and Bogota’s support will be essential to any sustained response to Venezuela’s crisis. Fentanyl and organized crime are high on the U.S.-Mexico agenda, and state failure in the Caribbean has often required immediate U.S. action. The more Washington has to manage those problems, the less attention it can devote elsewhere.

The American public is directly affected by events in those countries: manufacturing workers depend on North American supply chains; farmers and energy producers depend on regional markets and transportation networks; and communities across the United States suffer the consequences of illicit drugs. Although border states encounter migration most immediately, immigration is a national political issue. And diaspora communities sustain strong connections to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, Colombia, and Venezuela.

Over the next decade, U.S. policy should strengthen the regional foundations of American power by helping the countries in Greater North America become stronger economic and security partners. Trade rules and investment tools—including rules-of-origin cumulation and financing from the Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and the Export-Import Bank—can enhance Caribbean and northern South American contributions to North American production and supply chains. U.S. policymakers can reduce dangerous dependencies and bolster resilience by allowing qualifying inputs from those countries to count toward regional content requirements while financing the power, ports, and logistics needed to support production. To address irregular migration, Washington must address the failures of the underlying regional system, including the mismatch between American labor demands and lawful channels for entry.
